title: Economic Growth Models
description: Solow, AK, endogenous growth — what can sustain rising living standards

concepts.title: The Big Question
concepts.contentHtml:
Why are some countries rich and others poor? Why have some grown rapidly while others stagnated?

The differences are vast. Per capita GDP (PPP) ranges from ~$1,000 in the poorest countries to $100,000+ in the richest — a hundredfold gap. Lifetime outcomes — health, education, freedom — track these differences closely.

Most of human history saw little growth. Living standards in 1700 weren't dramatically different from those in 1500 or 1300. The take-off began ~1800 in Europe, spread unevenly.

Development economics asks: what drives the take-off, what sustains growth, what causes some countries to converge with rich ones while others fall further behind?

concepts.title: The Solow Model
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Solow's 1956 model is the workhorse of growth economics.

Output Y comes from labor L and capital K, plus technology A: Y = AF(K, L). Capital accumulates from saving and depreciates each period.

With diminishing returns to capital, each new unit of capital adds less. Eventually new investment just replaces depreciation, and capital stops growing. The economy reaches a steady state.

Predictions:

– Higher saving raises steady-state income but not long-run growth.

– Population growth reduces steady-state income per worker.

– Technology growth (A rising) is the only sustained source of per-capita growth.

The model says wealth differences come from differences in capital, technology, and labor. The hard part is explaining why technology differs so much across countries — Solow takes it as exogenous.

concepts.title: Convergence — Conditional or Not
concepts.contentHtml:
Solow predicts convergence: poor countries grow faster than rich ones, eventually catching up.

Logic: capital's marginal product is high where capital is scarce. Investment flows to high-return locations. Technologies copy across borders. Catch-up should be possible and rapid.

Empirical reality is messier. Unconditional convergence — poor countries growing faster on average — fails badly across the world. Many poor countries diverged from rich ones, especially in Africa.

Conditional convergence — countries with similar fundamentals (institutions, education, savings) converge — does hold. Among OECD countries, convergence is real and visible. Within US states, within EU regions, conditional convergence works.

The implication: convergence requires institutional and policy preconditions that not all countries have. Closing the gap takes more than capital flow — it requires institutional development.

concepts.title: Endogenous Growth
concepts.contentHtml:
Solow's exogenous technology is unsatisfying — what determines technology growth itself?

Endogenous growth theory (Romer 1986, 1990; Lucas 1988; Aghion-Howitt 1992) brought technology into the model.

Key insight: knowledge and ideas are non-rivalrous. Once invented, a recipe or formula can be used by everyone simultaneously without depletion. Unlike capital, knowledge doesn't have diminishing returns.

This produces increasing returns at the world level. Growth comes from R&D investment, education, and the spillovers between them. Public policy can affect long-run growth by subsidizing research, protecting intellectual property, and building human capital.

Romer's 2018 Nobel and the body of work it represents shifted growth economics from accumulation to ideas. Patents, R&D credits, university funding, and skilled-immigration policy all matter for the rate of idea production.

concepts.title: Why Growth Compounds
concepts.contentHtml:
The most important fact about growth: small differences in rates compound into vast differences in levels.

South Korea grew at ~7% per year from 1960 to 2000. Real per-capita GDP rose ~12-fold. From subsistence to OECD living standards in 40 years.

Sub-Saharan Africa's real per-capita GDP grew at well under 1% per year on average over the same period, with long stagnation after the mid-1970s. The gap with Korea widened from rough parity to more than 10×.

The arithmetic: 70/g% gives the doubling time. 7% growth doubles in 10 years; 2% growth doubles in 35; 1% growth doubles in 70.

This is why growth, not redistribution, has been the dominant driver of poverty reduction historically. The world poverty rate fell from ~40% in 1981 to ~10% in 2017, mostly through Chinese and Indian economic growth.

The implication: even small permanent increases in growth rates can transform welfare over generations. The challenge is finding the policies that produce them.

title: Poverty & Inequality
description: Measuring poverty, Gini and Lorenz, the Kuznets curve

concepts.title: Measuring Poverty
concepts.contentHtml:
Poverty measurement starts with a question: what counts as poor?

Absolute poverty: a fixed standard, often a basic-needs basket. The World Bank's international extreme poverty line was $2.15/day (2017 PPP) until June 2025, when it was raised to $3.00/day (2021 PPP). By the old line, about 700 million people lived in extreme poverty in 2024, down from ~2 billion in 1990; the new line counts over 800 million.

Relative poverty: a fraction of national median income. EU uses 60% of median. Captures inequality and social exclusion alongside material deprivation.

Multidimensional poverty: deprivation across multiple dimensions — health, education, living standards. The MPI (Alkire-Foster) is now widely used alongside income measures.

The choice of measure matters. Absolute poverty has fallen dramatically globally; relative poverty in rich countries has barely moved. Both are real; they're answering different questions.

concepts.title: The Lorenz Curve and Gini Coefficient
concepts.contentHtml:
To measure inequality, the Lorenz curve plots cumulative income share against cumulative population share.

Perfect equality is the diagonal — bottom 50% of population gets 50% of income, etc. Inequality bows the curve below the diagonal.

The Gini coefficient is twice the area between the diagonal and the curve. Ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything).

Country Ginis:

– Nordic countries: 0.25-0.28

– Continental Europe: 0.30-0.35

– UK, US: 0.35-0.40

– Latin America (mostly): 0.45-0.55

– South Africa: 0.63 (highest among major countries)

– Brazil: ~0.50

The Gini is one number summarizing a whole distribution — it's blind to where in the distribution inequality concentrates. Top-share statistics complement it.

concepts.title: The Kuznets Curve
concepts.contentHtml:
Simon Kuznets's 1955 hypothesis: inequality rises, then falls, as countries develop.

The Kuznets curve is an inverted U. Early industrialization concentrates returns in capital owners and skilled urban workers; late development sees the workforce shift to higher-productivity sectors and democratic redistribution kick in.

The hypothesis fit the experience of Western Europe and the US through the mid-20th century — inequality rising 1820-1920, falling 1920-1970.

Then it broke. Most rich countries saw inequality rise again from 1980 onward — driven by skill-biased technical change, globalization, financialization, declining unionization, and tax-policy shifts.

Piketty's Capital in the 21st Century proposed that the post-WWII compression was the historical exception, not the rule, and that high inequality is the default state of capitalism. The original Kuznets curve isn't holding up empirically; what comes next isn't settled.

concepts.title: Global Inequality
concepts.contentHtml:
There are two distinct inequality stories.

Within-country inequality: rising in most rich countries since 1980. Falling in some emerging markets (Brazil, parts of Latin America 2000-15).

Between-country inequality: falling sharply since 1990, mostly because China and India grew faster than rich countries.

Global inequality (treating all humans as one population): falling overall in recent decades, despite rising within-country inequality, because the between-country fall has dominated.

The 'elephant graph' (Lakner-Milanovic) shows the distribution of growth across the global income distribution, 1988-2008: large gains for the global middle (mostly Asia), stagnation for the lower-middle of rich countries (the political backdrop of 2010s populism), and very large gains for the global top 1%.

The 2020s may continue or reverse these patterns. China's slowing growth, India's acceleration, and African demographics will reshape the picture.

concepts.title: Inequality and Growth
concepts.contentHtml:
Does inequality help or hurt growth?

The traditional argument: some inequality is necessary for incentives to work. People need return for skill, effort, risk-taking. Pure equality blunts these.

The newer argument: extreme inequality may hurt growth. Mechanisms:

– Wealth concentration restricts effective demand (rich save more).

– Political capture by elites distorts policy.

– Children of the poor get less education and human capital investment.

– Social trust and cohesion erode at high inequality levels.

– Rent-seeking displaces productive activity.

Empirical evidence (Cingano, Berg-Ostry, IMF studies) suggests moderate inequality is neutral or weakly positive for growth, but high inequality is negative. The relationship is non-linear.

This complicates simple efficiency-equity tradeoffs. At low-to-moderate levels, more equality may be win-win; at extreme inequality, redistribution may help both.

The political-economy challenge: even when redistribution would help everyone, those whose taxes rise often have the most political power.

title: Institutions & Development
description: Acemoglu and Robinson — why nations fail, extractive vs inclusive institutions

concepts.title: Why Institutions Matter
concepts.contentHtml:
If technology and capital can flow across borders, why don't poor countries simply adopt rich-country recipes and catch up?

Because the preconditions for productive use of technology and capital differ across countries. Institutions — the rules of the game — are central.

Property rights, contract enforcement, rule of law, state capacity, financial systems, public goods provision — all are institutional features that determine whether a country can use available technology to actually generate growth.

This view dates back to Adam Smith and Hume but became formalized in modern economics through Douglass North's work on institutions and economic history (Nobel 1993), and crystallized in Acemoglu and Robinson's framework.

concepts.title: Extractive vs Inclusive Institutions
concepts.contentHtml:
Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson's framework (Nobel 2024) divides institutions into two categories.

Extractive institutions: concentrate power and resources in a small elite. Most subjects work for the benefit of that elite. Property rights are insecure for non-elites. Innovation threatens the elite's position, so it's discouraged.

Examples: colonial extractive states, Soviet command economies, kleptocratic dictatorships, much of Latin America historically, many resource-curse states.

Inclusive institutions: distribute political power broadly, protect property rights for many, allow free entry into economic activities, provide public goods, encourage education and innovation.

Examples: Western Europe post-WWII, US (with caveats — slavery was deeply extractive), Japan post-Meiji, South Korea post-1960s, Botswana.

Why does this matter? Because the same technologies and resources produce vastly different growth outcomes depending on institutional context.

concepts.title: Critical Junctures
concepts.contentHtml:
Institutions are persistent — they self-reinforce. Once extractive elites are in place, they have strong incentives and tools to keep institutions extractive. Once inclusive institutions develop, they create constituencies that defend them.

This persistence makes institutional change rare. Most countries follow trajectories set centuries ago.

But persistence isn't permanence. Critical junctures — moments of crisis or contingency — sometimes shift trajectories.

Examples: the Black Death weakened feudal labor relations in England and parts of Western Europe but strengthened them in Eastern Europe (the Second Serfdom). The Glorious Revolution of 1688 set British institutions on inclusive paths. The Meiji Restoration (1868) launched Japanese inclusive development. The collapse of communism in 1989 was a critical juncture for Eastern Europe with very different outcomes (Estonia inclusive, Russia largely extractive).

The lessons: institutional change is possible but contingent. Crises create openings; what fills them depends on the existing distribution of power and ideas.

concepts.title: Geography vs Institutions
concepts.contentHtml:
What's deeper — institutions or geography?

Jeffrey Sachs argued geography matters fundamentally: tropical disease, lack of arable land, landlocked locations all impose persistent constraints.

Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson (2001) used a clever empirical approach: where Europeans settled in colonies (good climate for them), they set up inclusive institutions. Where they didn't (high mortality), they set up extractive ones. Centuries later, the institutional pattern persists more strongly than the original mortality differences.

The conclusion: institutions explain more of the income gap than geography does — though geography influenced which institutions emerged.

The view that's emerged: geography shapes initial conditions; institutions shape long-run development; both interact and persist. Tropical countries, resource-rich or not, can be rich (Singapore, Brunei) or poor (DRC) depending on institutions. Land-locked mountain countries can be rich (Switzerland) or poor (Bhutan, Nepal). Geography is fate up to a point; institutions matter beyond that.

concepts.title: Implications for Policy
concepts.contentHtml:
If institutions are central, what's the policy lesson?

Sobering: institutional reform is hard. The elites that benefit from extractive institutions resist change. External advice (World Bank, IMF, USAID) can prescribe reforms but can't easily implement them locally.

Successful institutional reforms often follow:

– Crises that weaken existing elite coalitions.

– Domestic reform movements that build new political coalitions.

– External anchors that lock in changes (EU accession for Eastern Europe; WTO membership; binding international treaties).

– Patient sequencing: start with relatively easy reforms (macro stabilization, basic property rights) before harder ones (judiciary, anti-corruption, redistribution).

What clearly doesn't work: imposing institutional change from outside through military intervention or aid conditionality. The institutional record of US/UK regime change has been poor (Iraq, Afghanistan), and aid conditionality has frequently failed.

The hopeful note: many countries did transition successfully over the past 50-70 years (Korea, Taiwan, Spain, much of Eastern Europe, parts of Latin America, Botswana). Institutional development is possible — just slow and contingent.

title: RCTs & Field Experiments
description: Banerjee, Duflo, Kremer — randomization in development policy

concepts.title: The Randomization Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
Through most of development economics' history, evidence came from cross-country regressions and theory. Both have well-known limitations: confounders abound; theory only goes so far.

The 1990s and 2000s brought a methodological revolution: randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of development interventions in real settings.

Pioneered by Michael Kremer (deworming experiments in Kenya), Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee (J-PAL at MIT), and others — the 'randomista' movement won the 2019 Nobel.

The core idea: pick an intervention (a textbook program, a microcredit offer, a vaccination campaign), randomly assign it to some communities or individuals, compare outcomes. Random assignment ensures the comparison group is otherwise similar — the difference is the treatment effect.

This approach has produced thousands of evaluations across education, health, finance, governance, and agriculture. It's reshaped development practice.

concepts.title: Notable Findings
concepts.contentHtml:
RCTs produced a stream of policy-relevant findings — many surprising.

Deworming (Miguel-Kremer 2004): cheap deworming in Kenya cut school absenteeism by about a quarter and had measurable long-run effects on adult earnings. One of the most cost-effective interventions found.

Microcredit: large-scale RCTs across multiple countries (Banerjee, Duflo, others) found microcredit had small or zero effects on income for most borrowers — a major revision of the optimistic narrative around it.

Conditional cash transfers (Mexico's PROGRESA, evaluated rigorously from 1997): large positive effects on school attendance, child nutrition, immunization. Spread to dozens of countries.

Bednets: free distribution of insecticide-treated bednets dramatically reduced malaria. The economics of giving things away vs charging modest amounts (Cohen-Dupas 2010) showed free distribution worked far better.

Information interventions: simple information about returns to schooling, savings, vaccination produced significant behavioral changes.

concepts.title: External Validity
concepts.contentHtml:
RCTs deliver clean estimates of treatment effects in specific contexts. Whether the same intervention would work elsewhere is a separate question.

This is the external validity problem. An intervention that worked in rural Kenya might fail in urban Brazil. Same logic, different culture, different markets, different state capacity.

Approaches to extrapolation:

– Replication: run the same intervention in multiple contexts. If results are similar, evidence base strengthens. If they vary, you learn what context-features matter.

– Mechanism focus: identify why something worked (the underlying behavioral pathway) rather than just whether it worked. Mechanisms transfer better than effect sizes.

– Theory-guided extrapolation: combine RCT evidence with theoretical models to predict effects in untested settings.

Best practice has shifted toward multi-country, multi-context evaluations precisely to address external validity. The 'meta-analysis' of microcredit RCTs (Banerjee-Karlan-Zinman 2015) is a benchmark.

concepts.title: Critiques
concepts.contentHtml:
The randomization revolution has been controversial. Several critiques:

Scope. RCTs work for small, well-defined interventions. They can't easily evaluate national institutional reforms, monetary policy, trade liberalization, or major political changes — the things that may matter most for development. Lant Pritchett, Angus Deaton, and Dani Rodrik have argued the methodology limits attention to small-scale interventions.

Cherry-picking interventions: publication bias toward findings that 'work.' Many RCTs of programs that don't work go unreported.

Implementation gap: what's tested in tightly-monitored RCTs may not survive scaling to full government implementation, where supervision is weaker and incentives different.

Ethics: randomly denying potentially-beneficial interventions raises ethical questions, even with informed consent.

The mature view: RCTs are powerful but not the only tool. Combining them with structural models, quasi-experiments, and qualitative work produces better evidence than any approach alone.

concepts.title: What We've Learned
concepts.contentHtml:
Twenty-plus years of development RCTs have shifted thinking in several ways.

– Information matters more than expected. Simple information interventions can produce large behavior changes cheaply.

– Default options matter. Auto-enrollment in savings, immunization, school enrollment dramatically increases participation.

– Cash transfers are remarkably effective. Direct cash to poor households often outperforms more elaborate interventions.

– Free is better than cheap for products with positive externalities (vaccines, bednets).

– Behavioral barriers matter. Many development problems aren't about resources but about default behavior, present bias, social norms.

– Some popular programs fail. Microcredit, business training, agricultural extension — RCTs have repeatedly shown smaller effects than advocates claimed.

– Targeting matters. Same intervention can have very different effects across population subgroups; 'average treatment effects' often hide important heterogeneity.

The cumulative effect: development practitioners are more empirically rigorous than 25 years ago, more humble about which programs work, and more willing to scale evidence-backed interventions.

title: Industrialization & Structural Change
description: Lewis model, dual economies, import substitution vs export-led growth

concepts.title: Structural Transformation
concepts.contentHtml:
Economic development isn't just about getting richer at the same activities. It's about structural transformation — moving people and resources from low-productivity to high-productivity sectors.

Pre-industrial countries: ~80% in agriculture, ~10% manufacturing, ~10% services. Productivity is low across the board, especially in agriculture.

Industrialized countries: ~2% agriculture, ~20% manufacturing, ~78% services. Productivity is dramatically higher per worker.

The shift unlocks growth: workers moving from subsistence agriculture (where MP is near zero) to manufacturing (where MP is high) raise total output even without changing technology.

This pattern played out in 18th-19th century Britain, 19th-20th century Western Europe and US, late-20th century East Asia. It's playing out unevenly elsewhere.

concepts.title: The Lewis Model
concepts.contentHtml:
Arthur Lewis (Nobel 1979) modeled this as a dual economy.

Two sectors. Traditional (agriculture, informal): surplus labor with near-zero marginal product. Workers produce barely more than they consume.

Modern (manufacturing, formal): higher productivity, capital-intensive.

Modern-sector firms can hire from the traditional sector at a wage just above subsistence — there's effectively unlimited supply. Profits in the modern sector are reinvested, expanding capital and absorbing more workers.

The process continues until the surplus labor is exhausted — the Lewis turning point. After that, wages rise as labor becomes scarce, and growth shifts to a more conventional pattern.

China is widely thought to have passed its Lewis turning point between the mid-2000s and the 2010s (the exact date is debated). Manufacturing wages rose substantially; the country shifted from labor-intensive exports toward higher-value production.

concepts.title: Import Substitution Industrialization
concepts.contentHtml:
Mid-20th century Latin America (and parts of Asia, Africa) tried Import Substitution Industrialization (ISI): build domestic industry behind tariff walls, replacing imports with local production.

Logic: infant industry argument. Local producers can't compete initially with established foreign producers; protection gives them time to develop. Eventually they reach competitive levels and tariffs come down.

Practice: tariffs and quotas remained, often increasing over time. Protected industries became inefficient, never reaching competitive scale. State ownership and capital controls amplified inefficiency. Foreign exchange shortages were chronic.

By the 1980s, the ISI model had largely failed. The Latin American debt crisis exposed deep economic problems — high inflation, unsustainable government deficits, low productivity. Most countries shifted toward liberalization.

The lesson isn't that protection always fails — South Korea and Taiwan used substantial protection successfully. But protection without complementary policies (export discipline, productivity targets, sunset provisions) tends to entrench inefficiency rather than build competitiveness.

concepts.title: Export-Led Growth
concepts.contentHtml:
The East Asian alternative: export-led growth. Build industry to compete in world markets from the start.

The successful examples: Japan post-WWII, South Korea and Taiwan from the 1960s, Singapore and Hong Kong as city-states, China from 1978, Vietnam more recently.

Common features:

– Export discipline: firms must compete in world markets, generating learning and productivity pressure.

– Industrial policy targeting specific sectors (textiles → light manufacturing → heavy industry → electronics → high-tech).

– Macroeconomic stability: low inflation, fiscal discipline.

– High savings and investment rates (often 30%+ of GDP).

– Investment in human capital: universal basic education, then technical and tertiary expansion.

– Accommodating world markets: the postwar liberal trading system allowed these countries to export.

The model produced the fastest sustained growth in history: 8-10% per year over 30+ years. Per-capita GDP rose 10-30× in three to four decades.

concepts.title: Limits and Future Paths
concepts.contentHtml:
The export-led model is harder to replicate today than 30 years ago.

Reasons:

– Manufacturing is more capital-intensive than it was. Robotics and automation reduce employment per dollar of output.

– Existing low-cost producers (China especially) saturate many global markets. Latecomers face stiffer competition.

– The global trading system is fragmenting. US-China tensions, post-pandemic reshoring, climate-driven trade barriers all narrow the export window.

– Premature deindustrialization (Rodrik): poor countries are now seeing manufacturing employment shares peak at lower levels and earlier in development than rich countries did. They de-industrialize before fully industrializing.

What might work instead?

– Services-led growth (India's IT sector model).

– Resource-driven development with strong institutions (Norway, Botswana).

– Domestic-market manufacturing for large countries (India, Indonesia, Brazil).

– Climate-related industries (renewable energy, electric vehicles, green hydrogen).

No clear successor model has emerged. The next generation of developing countries will be inventing as they go.
